claims.statement: Dorothea Lange was born Dorothea Margaretta Nutzhorn in Hoboken, New Jersey, on May 26, 1895.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Sources differ on the day: May 26 (New Jersey Hall of Fame and the PBS biography summary), May 25 (the PBS timeline), and May 15 (a Gale reference biography). May 26 is preferred.

claims.statement: At the age of seven, in 1902, Lange had polio, which left her with a weakened right leg and a lifelong limp.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A reference biography describes a withered right leg after recovery from the paralysis; a review of her standard biography says it left her right foot twisted. The documented paralytic polio is the first March of Dimes criterion for post-polio syndrome.

claims.statement: In her oral history of 1960 to 1961 Lange said: "I was physically disabled, and no one who hasn't lived the life of a semi-cripple knows how much that means. I think it perhaps was the most important thing that happened to me, and formed me, guided me, instructed me, helped me, and humiliated me."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own words; quoted from the transcript.

claims.statement: In the same interview Lange said that her lameness as a child, and her acceptance of it, "truly opened gates for me", and that working among strangers as a disabled person gave "an immense advantage. People are kinder."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own account of how disability shaped her work; the synthetic episode protects that work.

claims.statement: Lange was a documentary photographer. In 1935 she was hired as a photographer for the Resettlement Administration, later the Farm Security Administration, and in March 1936 she made the photograph known as "Migrant Mother" in Nipomo, California. From the mid-1930s she lived in Berkeley, California.
In the late 1940s ill health stopped Lange working: she had a succession of severe stomach ulcers that were controlled only by radical surgery, and pain and discomfort troubled her from then on.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The type of operation is not given in the sources read; the record says only that she had surgery for stomach ulcers.

claims.statement: In the early 1950s Lange returned to work with photographic essays for Life and Fortune and helped to found the photography magazine Aperture; her poor health limited her to short bursts of work.
From 1958 she traveled widely abroad with her husband, in Asia, the Middle East, and South America, although poor health and unfamiliar languages made the work hard.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Later than the synthetic episode and not used in it.

claims.statement: A review of her standard biography says that bleeding ulcers and esophageal problems troubled Lange as she grew older, so that she often had difficulty eating.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The review gives no dates; the record links this only to a later timeline event and does not use it in the synthetic episode.

claims.statement: The same review says that Lange developed post-polio symptoms in late middle age and that post-polio fatigue tired her.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Post-polio syndrome was not described as a condition until after her death, so this is a retrospective interpretation by her biographer as summarized in a review; the dates and findings are not given. The synthetic episode makes the modern diagnosis but does not assert it as historical.

claims.statement: In 1964 Lange was diagnosed with inoperable cancer of the esophagus.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Later than the synthetic episode and not used in it. The synthetic reflux evaluation does not foreshadow it.

claims.statement: Knowing she was dying, Lange spent her last months preparing a retrospective of her life's work at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, which opened in January 1966.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Later than the synthetic episode and not used in it.

claims.statement: Lange died of cancer in San Francisco on October 11, 1965, at 70.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail.

claims.statement: After her death her personal archive, more than 40,000 negatives and 6,000 prints, was given to the Oakland Museum of California.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize post-polio syndrome as a diagnosis of exclusion in a woman of 61 with new fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, and falls 55 years after paralytic polio: apply the modified March of Dimes criteria, confirm prior polio and exclude neuropathy and myopathy with nerve conduction and EMG, and exclude thyroid disease, anemia, diabetes, B12 deficiency, depression, and sleep-disordered breathing. Manage it as the EFNS guideline advises, with energy conservation and pacing, supervised non-fatiguing exercise, a lightweight ankle-foot orthosis and cane, fall prevention, respiratory and sleep assessment, pain care without NSAIDs, bone health, and sedation precautions, while protecting her work as a photographer in the field. Evaluate reflux symptoms that return off a proton pump inhibitor with an upper endoscopy off therapy, as the 2022 ACG guidelines advise, and act on the findings.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Lange returns 16 days after presenting with about 18 months of new fatigue, slowly increasing weakness of the left leg and both shoulders as well as her polio-affected right leg, aching after field work, and two falls. Her blood tests at the first visit excluded the common other causes: hemoglobin 13.1, TSH 2.1, HbA1c 5.4 percent, B12 512, creatinine 0.7, ESR 12, and CRP 0.3 were normal; creatine kinase was mildly raised at 228 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D low at 22. Her PHQ-9 was 6. Nerve conduction studies a week ago were normal, and the needle EMG showed chronic reinnervation in the right leg and, more mildly, in the left thigh and right shoulder, with no myopathy. She saw Dr. Haddad-Sorensen this morning, who confirmed post-polio syndrome. Today she had a bone density scan and spirometry. Her heartburn is much better after two weeks of omeprazole. She asked plainly whether this would keep getting worse and whether she would have to stop working in the field.

She completed the eight-week omeprazole trial two weeks ago and stopped it; within five days the heartburn and regurgitation came back on three or four nights a week. She has no difficulty swallowing, weight loss, vomiting, or black stools. She has taken vitamin D3 daily, saw her dentist last month with no problems, and has not yet returned the 24-hour urine collection: she was away photographing for two weeks.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Lange had an upper endoscopy two and a half weeks ago, three and a half weeks after her last omeprazole dose, under moderate sedation at reduced doses with oxygen and carbon dioxide monitoring and warming; she recovered without any fall in oxygen saturation. The fever and aching after the zoledronic acid infusion settled in three days. Heartburn continues on four or five nights a week on antacid tablets. Physical therapy ends next week; she has learned her home program. No falls. She is printing in the darkroom for an exhibition and photographing two days a week.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Lange is a 61-year-old photographer with post-polio syndrome and osteoporosis who had her first infusion of zoledronic acid 5 mg two days ago. Yesterday afternoon, about 24 hours after the infusion, she developed a temperature of 38.1 °C, aching in her thighs, shoulders, and knees, a dull headache, and tiredness. She has no cough, sore throat, burning on passing urine, rash, or diarrhea, and no numbness or tingling around the mouth or cramps in her hands. She took acetaminophen 1000 mg twice with partial relief and has been drinking well. She was worried that the aching meant her polio-affected muscles were getting worse, and asked whether she should cancel a field day next week.

referral.question: New fatigue, slowly increasing weakness in the left leg and both arms as well as the right leg weakened by paralytic polio at seven, muscle aching after work, and two falls, over about 18 months, in a photographer of 61. Is this post-polio syndrome, and how should she be managed so that she can keep working?
referral.pertinent_history: Polio at seven left a weak right leg and a limp; she recovered enough to walk without an aid and has worked for decades, often standing for hours with heavy cameras. For about 18 months she has tired after two hours of activity and noticed weakness in the left leg and both shoulders, with aching in the thighs and shoulders after field days, a cold right foot, and two falls from catching the right foot, without injury. No numbness, swallowing trouble, or breathlessness; sleep is unrefreshing. On examination the right leg is thin with foot drop and knee hyperextension; Timed Up and Go 14 seconds. Same-day blood tests are sent (blood count, chemistry, glucose and HbA1c, TSH, B12, vitamin D, calcium, creatine kinase, ESR, and CRP), and nerve conduction studies and needle EMG are booked; PHQ-9 6. An operation for stomach ulcers in her early fifties, so no NSAIDs. Heartburn for three months, starting an omeprazole trial; endoscopy may be needed. No known allergy. She wants to keep photographing in the field

consultant_note.history: Ms. Lange is seen at the request of Dr. Ashford-Mensah. She had polio at seven, with weakness of the right leg from which she partly recovered; she walked without an aid for more than 50 years and worked long days on her feet carrying cameras. Over about 18 months she has developed fatigue after two hours of activity, weakness of the left thigh and both shoulders, increased weakness of the right leg, aching after work, cold intolerance of the right foot, and two falls from catching the right foot. She has no sensory symptoms, swallowing trouble, breathlessness, or morning headaches; her sleep is unrefreshing. She asked for a plain answer about whether she would have to stop working

exam.finding: Right calf and thigh thinner than the left; high-arched right foot; right knee hyperextends in stance

Strength (MRC): right hip abductors 4-/5, right quadriceps 3+/5, right ankle dorsiflexion 2/5, right plantar flexion 3/5; left quadriceps 4/5, left hip abductors 4/5; deltoids 4+/5 on both sides. Reflexes absent at the right knee and ankle. Sensation normal. No fasciculations

Normal chest expansion and cough

assessment.assessment: She meets the modified March of Dimes criteria. Prior paralytic polio is confirmed by history, examination, and EMG, which shows chronic reinnervation in the right leg and, more mildly, in the left vastus lateralis and right deltoid, so polio affected more muscles than she knew. Partial recovery was followed by decades of stable function, and the new weakness and fatigue have lasted more than a year. Normal nerve conduction excludes neuropathy and entrapment, the EMG shows no myopathy and no decrement on repetitive stimulation, and the blood tests exclude thyroid disease, anemia, diabetes, B12 deficiency, and inflammation; the mildly raised creatine kinase fits overuse. Depression is mild and secondary. No drug has a proven effect on post-polio syndrome, so pyridostigmine, amantadine, and corticosteroids are not recommended

Supervised, individualized training at submaximal effort improves strength, fatigue, and pain without harming motor units if it does not cause exhaustion or aching the next day. Warm-water exercise suits her cold intolerance

Both falls come from right foot drop, and the knee hyperextension strains the knee. A custom lightweight carbon-fiber ankle-foot orthosis will clear the foot and control the knee, and is light enough to wear on field days; a cane in the left hand unloads the right leg. A knee-ankle-foot orthosis is not needed now because the knee does not buckle

No breathlessness or bulbar symptoms, a normal cough, and normal spirometry today make respiratory muscle weakness unlikely. Unrefreshing sleep should be screened with home overnight oximetry; sleep apnea and nocturnal hypoventilation are more common in polio survivors

Polio survivors can be sensitive to sedatives, opioids, and neuromuscular blocking drugs and may have unrecognized respiratory weakness, cold intolerance, and positioning problems. For an endoscopy, moderate sedation at reduced doses with oxygen and carbon dioxide monitoring is appropriate

Post-polio syndrome usually progresses slowly, over years, and pacing, the right exercise, and an orthosis often stabilize function or improve it. She can keep working in the field with planned rest and less to carry

recommendations: Twelve weeks of supervised physical therapy, twice a week: submaximal strengthening with rest days, aerobic and warm-water exercise, gait and balance training, and energy conservation; then a home program. Stop any exercise that leaves her exhausted or aching the next day
Custom lightweight carbon-fiber right ankle-foot orthosis, fitted within four weeks, and a single-point cane in the left hand
Pacing for field days: a lighter camera on a harness, a seat stick, an assistant to carry the tripod, rest breaks every hour, and a rest day after each field day
Baseline spirometry today, then yearly or with symptoms; home overnight oximetry for unrefreshing sleep

Record sedation and anesthesia precautions in the chart: reduced sedative and opioid doses, continuous oxygen and carbon dioxide monitoring, warming, careful positioning of the right leg, and caution with neuromuscular blocking drugs
No disease-specific drug; acetaminophen, heat, and pacing for pain; no NSAIDs after her ulcer surgery

Bone density of both hips and the spine, since disuse of the right leg and falls raise fracture risk; the scan done today by primary care shows osteoporosis of the right hip, which primary care will treat
Review in this clinic at six months, or sooner for new weakness, breathlessness, or swallowing trouble
